text: Sears got here first. It opened standing alone on this lot in 1966. The mall was built onto it three years later.
The movies beat the mall too. The 600-seat Southland Cinema opened July 17, 1968, seven months before the mall's grand opening.
Southland opened in late February 1969 at the height of the oil boom. Old clippings can't agree on the day: Feb. 26 or Feb. 28.
The whole mall opened with just 14 stores, including Sears, K&B, Woolworth, Winn-Dixie and D.H. Holmes.
Grand-opening grand prize, 1969: an all-expenses-paid trip for two to Mexico City.
Houma's very first escalator was inside D.H. Holmes, around 1970. It was such an event that WWL-TV sent a crew.
Before Southland, Houma shoppers drove to Thibodaux, Morgan City, or all the way to New Orleans.
Before Houma had a civic center, the mall was the biggest room in town: orchid shows, book fairs and fashion shows with local girls as models.
For its first decade Southland had only 20 to 25 stores. The 1981 wing added JCPenney and room for 35 more.
The mall you're walking through got its look in 1994, when owner Sizeler remodeled it inside and out.
In 1996 the books valued Southland at about $41.8 million and it was 96% leased.
Connie Parr ran the mall's marketing for 15 years, 1981 to 1996, from the JCPenney wing through the big remodel.
Dillard's added a third floor in 1997, making it the only multi-level piece of an otherwise one-story mall.
At its 40th birthday in 2009 the mall covered 625,000 square feet on 29 acres, with about 1,500 people working inside.
The original anchor outlived the mall's first owner: Sears closed its 1966 building in July 2016, after 50 years.
The first movie ever shown at Southland Cinema was El Dorado with John Wayne, in July 1968. The last, in 2000, was Gone in 60 Seconds.
In 1995 the theater was the UA Southland Cinema 4, a four-screen run by United Artists since 1986.
Two locals reopened the cinema as a $1.95 discount house in 2004. It closed for good in 2007 over a $40,000 air-conditioning repair.
Before it was a Dillard's it was a D.H. Holmes, the New Orleans store founded on Canal Street in 1840. Dillard's bought the chain in 1989.
"Meet me under the clock" was the D.H. Holmes catchphrase. A Confederacy of Dunces opens with Ignatius Reilly standing under it.
William T. Dillard opened his first store on Feb. 12, 1938 in Nashville, Arkansas, at age 23, with $8,000 lent by his father.
A week after Dillard bought a Tulsa department store in 1960, someone found a cigar box holding $150,000 in unpaid bills.
JCPenney was downtown on Main Street before it was at the mall. It moved to Southland with the new wing in 1981.
James Cash Penney opened his first store in 1902 in Kemmerer, Wyoming, a coal town full of saloons. First-day sales: $466. He lived upstairs.
Sam Walton's first retail job was at a JCPenney in Des Moines in 1940.
When Sears dropped its catalog in 1993, JCPenney became America's biggest catalog retailer overnight.
Sears began in 1886 when a Minnesota railroad agent resold a shipment of watches a jeweler had refused. The first catalog was 80 pages of watches.
Sears killed its big catalog on Jan. 25, 1993, two years before this mall is set. The same day it closed 113 stores and cut 50,000 jobs.
The Sears catalog once sold 55,000 sets of Encyclopaedia Britannica in a single year, and about 70,000 mail-order houses between 1908 and 1940.
"Come see the softer side of Sears" launched in 1993. Sears lost $3.9 billion in 1992 and made $1.8 billion in 1995.
K&B stands for Katz and Besthoff, two druggists who opened the first store at 732 Canal Street in New Orleans in 1905.
Why was K&B purple? Years ago the company bought a bulk lot of purple wrapping paper, and it stuck. Even the liquor labels went purple.
K&B sold its ice cream as a loss leader, with more butterfat than the national brands. Creole cream cheese was a favorite flavor.
K&B sold to Rite Aid in 1997. Rite Aid's first move was dropping Coca-Cola from the shelves, which went over badly in New Orleans.
Sydney Besthoff's art collection became the sculpture garden at the New Orleans Museum of Art. The purple drugstore bought the sculptures.
Woolworth was an opening-day tenant here in 1969. In July 1997 the company closed all 400 remaining U.S. Woolworths, ending the five-and-dime after 118 years.
Frank Woolworth's first five-cent store failed in three months. The second, opened in Lancaster, Pennsylvania in June 1879, started a 118-year run.
Woolworth paid cash for the Woolworth Building in 1913, then the tallest building in the world.
When the last Woolworths closed in 1997, the lunch counters and soda fountains were sold off as collectibles.
Corn Dog 7 was started in 1978 by the McKinney family of Laurel, Mississippi. The first stand opened in 1981 at Sawmill Square Mall.
Why "7"? There were seven people in Stephen McKinney's family growing up.
Cheese on a stick is exactly what it sounds like: a block of American cheese dipped in corn dog batter and fried.
Corn Dog 7 once had stands in dozens of Southern malls. Today only three survive: two in Laurel, Mississippi and the one here at Southland.
Chick-fil-A was a mall-only restaurant for nearly 20 years. The first opened in 1967 in Atlanta's Greenbriar Mall in just 384 square feet.
Before there was a single Chick-fil-A, the sandwich was sold at the Houston Astrodome and licensed to Waffle House.
The capital A in Chick-fil-A is for Grade A. Truett Cathy picked a misspelled name because misspellings are easier to trademark.
The "Eat Mor Chikin" cows showed up on Atlanta billboards in 1995, the year this mall is set. The first one was a cow holding a paintbrush.
Closed on Sunday since 1946: the rule goes back to Truett Cathy's first diner, which took in $58.20 on its first day.
Karmelkorn started in Casper, Wyoming, where the O'Sullivans patented their candy-coated popcorn in 1929. Within four years 535 shops sold it.
Orange Julius began as a 1926 Los Angeles juice stand making $20 a day. A secret frothing powder pushed it to $100 a day.
Orange Julius was the official drink of the 1964 World's Fair. Its devil mascot was retired after Arizona State fans said it looked like their Sparky.
Great American Cookie opened in 1977 on $8,000. Landlords thought a cookie-only store was a joke; it did $30,000 in its first month.
The Cookie Cake is a Great American Cookie invention.
Cucos was a Metairie chain that started in 1981. The Houma location opened in September 1992: 6,000 square feet and 148 seats.
Cucos slogans over the years: "Alotta Enchilada" and "We Grill to Thrill." The Border Cafe name was trademarked in 1991.
The Pocket Change name was first used for coin-op arcades on April 1, 1989. Namco later bought the chain.
Southland's Pocket Change is still open today, outliving nearly every other mall arcade in the country.
Kay-Bee started in 1922 as Kaufman Brothers, a wholesale candy company in Massachusetts. K.B. is just the brothers' initials.
Kay-Bee got into toys by accident: a customer paid off his candy debt with a toy wholesaler, and wartime sugar rationing did the rest.
Around 1994 Kay-Bee pulled realistic toy guns and burned 300,000 of them, generating enough electricity to power 48 homes for a month.
Babbage's was founded in Dallas in 1983 and named for Charles Babbage, the Victorian who imagined the computer. Ross Perot bankrolled it.
The Babbage's you're looking at is a GameStop in disguise. It relaunched under the GameStop name in 1999.
Blockbuster Music was brand new in 1995: Blockbuster bought the Sound Warehouse chain for $185 million in 1992 and put its name on it.
A 1994 Blockbuster Music had dozens of headphone listening posts and a wall where you could sample the Top 20.
B. Dalton is "Dayton" with one letter changed. Bruce Dayton of the department-store family started it in 1966.
Radio Shack is named after a literal shack: the wooden hut that housed a ship's radio. Two brothers started it in Boston in 1921.
Tandy, a Fort Worth leather company, bought the nine-store, nearly bankrupt Radio Shack in 1963 for $300,000.
For decades Radio Shack's Battery of the Month club gave you a free battery every month for showing a punch card.
Mark and Brenda Felger took over Felger's at its original Southland spot in 1991, a 1,000-square-foot children's shoe store.
Duncan Sports was a family chain founded in Thibodaux in 1943. The last Houma store closed after Katrina.
Les Wexner opened the first Limited in 1963 with $5,000 borrowed from his aunt. It aimed for $100,000 its first year and did $162,000.
The Forenza label at The Limited credited its designer, Maria Pia. She didn't exist.
Lerner Shops dates to 1918. Co-founder Joseph Lerner's son was Alan Jay Lerner, who wrote the words to My Fair Lady.
Lane Bryant is a typo. Founder Lena Bryant opened her shop in 1904; a bank clerk wrote "Lane" on her account form and it stuck.
No newspaper would print a maternity-clothes ad until Lane Bryant talked the New York Herald into one in 1911. The shop sold out the next day.
Rave and Jean Nicole were both Petrie Stores banners. Petrie Retail went bankrupt on Oct. 12, 1995, so both shops were run out of a bankruptcy court.
Merry-Go-Round was founded in 1968 by Leonard "Boogie" Weinglass, the real-life model for Mickey Rourke's Boogie in the movie Diner.
Merry-Go-Round filed for bankruptcy in 1994 and liquidated in February 1996. In 1995 the Houma store was living on borrowed time.
5-7-9 is named for junior dress sizes 5, 7 and 9.
JW is short for Jeans West, a pants chain Edison Brothers bought in 1968 as its first clothing store.
The five Edison brothers named their first shoe store Chandler's after a car so the family name wouldn't suffer if it flopped. Bakers followed in 1924.
In 1999 grandson Peter Edison bought Bakers for $8 million about an hour before it was to be liquidated.
County Seat was started in 1973 by the CEO of a grocery company, and the name is a pun on jeans. By 1993 jeans were more than half of its sales.
Gadzooks opened in 1983 in a former waterbed store in a Mesquite, Texas mall, after the founder's teenage sons couldn't find clothes they liked.
The VW Beetle in every Gadzooks started as filler to cover empty floor. Dozens of Beetles were later sawed in half for displays.
Gadzooks went public in October 1995 at around $13 a share and quadrupled to $61 in three months.
Miller's Outpost was founded in 1972 by Dave Miller, whose family surplus store in California was famous for Levi's. It became Anchor Blue in 2001.
Foot Locker, Lady Foot Locker, Champs, Footquarters and the Woolworth down the hall all had the same owner in 1995: F.W. Woolworth.
The first Foot Locker opened in 1974 at a California mall as a side project of Kinney Shoes. The referee stripes didn't arrive until 1988.
Champs Sports grew out of Robby's Sporting Goods, a Florida family chain that Woolworth bought in the late 1980s.
Footaction was founded in Texas in 1976 by a 57-year-old ex-WWII pilot. His first name for it was "Webmit," for "We Better Make It."
The Athlete's Foot opened in Pittsburgh in 1971 as the first store selling only athletic shoes. The founder thought of the name at 4 a.m. and woke his wife.
Payless began in 1956 in a former Topeka supermarket, with managers building the shelves themselves. The average shoe cost under $3.
A tornado flattened Payless's Topeka headquarters the very evening its first computerized inventory report was due.
Naturalizer, born in 1927, was the first shoe built on a woman's last rather than a scaled-down man's.
The Shoe Dept's parent began in 1960 when Robert Tucker, a former curb boy at his stepfather's tavern, opened one store in Kannapolis, North Carolina.
Gordon's was one of Southland's 14 opening-day stores in 1969, and it's still here on the 1995 map.
Gordon's started in Houston in 1905 as a general store where jewelry was a sideline. In 1968 it became the first jeweler on the New York Stock Exchange.
Zales and Gordon's were rivals until 1989, when Zale bought Gordon's for $400 million. The debt helped push Zale into bankruptcy in 1992.
Morris Zale's first shop was a corner of a Texas drugstore, where he blasted a Victrola out front to pull in customers.
Zale's famous credit terms, from 1924: a penny down and a dollar a week.
Claire's was built by a high-school dropout whose first company was the world's largest seller of fashion wigs. Ear piercing didn't start until 1978.
Afterthoughts belonged to Woolworth. It had 809 stores in 1996 and was sold to Claire's in 1999.
Wicks 'n' Sticks was founded in Houston in 1968 with a stock of 23 scented candles. It peaked at 305 stores in 1988.
Wicks 'n' Sticks sold wax cheeseburgers so realistic that shoppers kept scratching them, so stores posted a sign: the candles don't itch.
GNC started in 1935 as "Lackzoom," a Pittsburgh store that mostly sold yogurt. First-day sales: $35.
The GNC Gold Card cost $15 a year in 1996 and got you 20% off on the first Tuesday of every month. It had 2.4 million members.
Regis and MasterCuts were the same company. Regis began in 1922 as Kunin Beauty Salons in Minneapolis and moved into malls in the 1960s.
MasterCuts launched in 1985 as Regis's no-frills brand for men and kids. By 1994 there were 257 of them.
By 1995 Glamour Shots had 380 studios on three continents. A high-school grad package with hair, makeup and wardrobe ran $199.
Only about 5% of Glamour Shots customers were men.
